title: Sliding Expiration
description: Implement sliding expiration to keep active users logged in while still expiring inactive sessions.

blocks.text: Sliding expiration is a session management strategy where the expiration time of a token is extended each time the user is actively using the application. Instead of a fixed expiration date, each refresh or activity event pushes the expiration forward by a configured window. Inactive users are eventually logged out, while active users remain authenticated seamlessly.

blocks.title: Analogy
blocks.text: Think of sliding expiration like a library book renewal. As long as you keep renewing the book, you can keep it. If you stop renewing, the book eventually expires and must be returned.

cards.title: Absolute Expiration
cards.description: The token expires at a fixed time regardless of activity.
cons: Active users get logged out unexpectedly
Poor user experience for long tasks

cards.title: Sliding Expiration
cards.description: The token expiration moves forward with each use, keeping active sessions alive.
cons: Inactive sessions can live indefinitely without limits

blocks.text: With sliding expiration, each time the client refreshes its access token using a refresh token, the refresh token expiration is pushed forward. For example, if the sliding window is 30 minutes and the refresh token is used at minute 25 of its life, it now expires at minute 55. If the refresh token is never used again, it expires at its original time.

blocks.text: Sliding expiration is implemented in the refresh token endpoint. When a refresh request is received, check the current refresh token expiration. If it is within a certain threshold of expiring, issue a new refresh token with a fresh expiration. Otherwise, return a new access token but keep the same refresh token. Always enforce a maximum absolute lifetime to prevent tokens from sliding forever.

blocks.content: Express implementation that extends refresh token expiration on each use.

blocks.title: Guidelines for Window Size
items: Match the window to your access token lifetime plus a small buffer (e.g., access token = 15 min, window = 30 min)
Shorter windows force more frequent refreshes, improving security but reducing convenience
Longer windows keep users logged in longer but increase the window for token theft
Consider user expectations: if users expect to work for hours, use a longer window

blocks.title: Maximum Absolute Lifetime
blocks.text: Always enforce a maximum absolute lifetime on refresh tokens, even with sliding expiration. Without this limit, an active user could stay logged in indefinitely, which violates most security policies.

Clients should proactively refresh access tokens before they expire. A common pattern is to refresh when the access token has less than 5 minutes remaining. When the server returns a new refresh token, the client must update its stored token. If the refresh fails, the client should redirect the user to the login page.

blocks.title: Key Takeaways
points: Sliding expiration extends the refresh token lifetime with each use
Combine sliding expiration with a maximum absolute lifetime
Implement sliding logic on the server during token refresh
Proactively refresh access tokens on the client before they expire
Set the sliding window to match access token lifetime plus a buffer
blocks.takeaway: Sliding expiration keeps active users authenticated while still ensuring inactive sessions eventually expire, striking the right balance between security and user experience.
